\chapter{Ground Underfoot}
\label{ch:ml-ground-underfoot}
\hlchaptermodality{55}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five features of the Kerala landscape in Malayalam.}

Complete ML-C55-field and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[puḻa]{\ml{പുഴ} (puḻa) — a river}

\label{lesson:ML-C55-river}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{vērŭ} mean, and what did \emph{vittŭ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{പുഴ}}
\textbf{\ml{പുഴ}} (\emph{puḻa}) — \textquotedblleft{}a river\textquotedblright{}.

Inherited, and it carries \ml{ഴ} — the sound Kannada and Telugu both lost, and the one this book has already pointed at as Malayalam's signature.

Kerala has forty-four rivers running west off the hills, and their names end in this word: Bharatappuzha, Chaliyar-puzha, Periyar. Reading a Kerala map is largely a matter of hearing \ml{പുഴ} at the end of things.

The borrowed \ml{നദി} (\emph{nadi}) is the formal one, and it is what a textbook prints. \ml{പുഴ} is what somebody points at.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five things underfoot.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{puḻa}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{vittŭ}, then \emph{puḻa}, and hold the \ml{ഴ} a moment longer than feels natural
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{പുഴ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a river\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pāṟa]{\ml{പാറ} (pāṟa) — a rock}

\label{lesson:ML-C55-rock}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{puḻa} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{പാറ}}
\textbf{\ml{പാറ}} (\emph{pāṟa}) — \textquotedblleft{}a rock\textquotedblright{}.

Inherited, matching Tamil \emph{pāṟai}. The hard \ml{റ} in the middle is the trilled one, and it separates this word from its neighbours by that sound alone.

Kerala's ground is laterite over granite, and \ml{പാറ} names the bare grey shoulders of it that show through where the soil has washed off. Quarrying is a \ml{പാറ} trade, and the word turns up on lorries and on hillsides both.

It goes figurative in the direction you would expect: somebody unmoved by argument has a heart of \ml{പാറ}, which is the same picture English reaches for and reached for separately.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: the water, and what it runs over.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pāṟa}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{puḻa}, then \emph{pāṟa}, and hear the soft sound against the hard one
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{പാറ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a rock\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nāṭŭ]{\ml{നാട്} (nāṭŭ) — home country, the place you are from}

\label{lesson:ML-C55-homeland}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{pāṟa} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{നാട്}}
\textbf{\ml{നാട്}} (\emph{nāṭŭ}) — \textquotedblleft{}home country, the place you are from\textquotedblright{}.

Inherited, matching Tamil \emph{nāṭu}, and it is one of the busiest words in the language. A \ml{നാട്} is a country, a district, a home region, or simply where you are from — the scale floats, and the situation fixes it.

It sits inside place-names all over the south, and inside the everyday question a Malayali asks a stranger early in a conversation: which \ml{നാട്} are you from. Answering with a village is as correct as answering with a country.

Its opposite is \ml{കാട്} (\emph{kāṭŭ}), the forest — settled ground against wild ground, one vowel apart, and the pair is old enough to be shared right across the family.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, and this one is the question you get asked.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nāṭŭ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{nāṭŭ}, then \emph{kāṭŭ}, and hear how little separates the tame from the wild
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{നാട്} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}home country, the place you are from\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vaḻi]{\ml{വഴി} (vaḻi) — a way, a path}

\label{lesson:ML-C55-path}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{nāṭŭ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{വഴി}}
\textbf{\ml{വഴി}} (\emph{vaḻi}) — \textquotedblleft{}a way, a path\textquotedblright{}.

Inherited, matching Tamil \emph{vaḻi}, and another \ml{ഴ} word — the second in this run, which tells you how deep that sound sits in the oldest layer of the language.

\ml{വഴി} is a path you walk and also a means by which something happens. Malayalam uses it where English says \emph{by way of} and \emph{through}, so a letter can come by \ml{വഴി} of a friend.

The road and the method being one word is not peculiar to Malayalam. English \emph{way} does the same double duty, and so does the Latin piece behind \emph{via}. Some pictures are simply obvious to everybody.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four: the river, the rock, the home place, and the way through it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vaḻi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{puḻa}, then \emph{vaḻi}, and hold the \ml{ഴ} in both
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{വഴി} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a way, a path\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vayal]{\ml{വയൽ} (vayal) — a paddy field}

\label{lesson:ML-C55-field}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{vaḻi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{വയൽ}}
\textbf{\ml{വയൽ}} (\emph{vayal}) — \textquotedblleft{}a paddy field\textquotedblright{}.

Inherited, matching Tamil \emph{vayal}, and it names a particular kind of field: the flooded, bunded one where rice grows. Dry ground planted with something else takes a different word.

That specificity is the point. A language grown in a rice country puts its sharpest word on the wet field, and Kuttanad — the stretch of Kerala farmed below sea level — is \ml{വയൽ} for miles in every direction.

The chillu \ml{ൽ} closing it is the one you met on the door-word and the leg-word, a bare \emph{l} with no vowel behind it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five, and the ground is furnished: a river, a rock, the home place, a way, a paddy field.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vayal}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{puḻa}, \emph{pāṟa}, \emph{nāṭŭ}, \emph{vaḻi}, \emph{vayal}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{വയൽ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a paddy field\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
